strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: scalable GRN discovery from large perturbational single-cell datasets, including dynamic differentiation settings where static DAG-based causal models are limited.

The proposed PerturbODE architecture is conceptually appealing: a neural ODE with biologically motivated decay, sigmoid/Hill-like module activations, intervention inputs, and a low-rank/module factorization that gives a plausible route to scalability and interpretability.
The manuscript evaluates on both SERGIO simulations and a large TF Atlas overexpression dataset, and includes comparisons to several relevant causal discovery baselines when they can run.

The held-out perturbation experiment is a useful addition beyond graph recovery, and PerturbODE shows substantially better Pearson correlation than the linear SCM baselines on those ten interventions.

The appendices include many implementation details, hyperparameters, thresholding choices, ablations over modules/regularization/number of perturbations, and biological module analyses, which improves transparency.
weaknesses: The central GRN discovery evidence is not yet convincing. On SERGIO, PerturbODE does not outperform DCDI, and absolute AUPRC values for the 400-gene yeast network appear very low. The method is positioned as causal GRN discovery, but the strongest empirical result is scalability and prediction rather than accurate edge recovery.

Thresholded graph results are highly sensitive and sometimes troubling: PerturbODE predicts 43,655 edges for a 623-edge yeast ground truth and about 101,404 edges on TF Atlas. The paper acknowledges overprediction, but this weakens the interpretability and causal discovery claims substantially.

The TF Atlas evaluation uses only known positive edges, so recall and p-values against Erdos-Renyi random graphs do not establish precision or causal correctness. A dense graph can obtain high recall, and the random-graph null is too weak a comparator for biological network recovery.

The held-out intervention evaluation is limited: only ten randomly held-out TFs, apparently one split, and comparison only to relatively weak linear SCM baselines because other methods cannot sample. PerturbODE also has very high W2 variance and is worse than NO-TEARS-LR on several held-out TFs, so the generalization claim is only partially supported.

The theoretical/causal justification is underdeveloped. Identifiability is described as delicate and deferred to future work or an anonymized 2025 reference; the equivalence to SCMs via stable fixed points is asserted but not made rigorous enough to support the causal interpretation of learned parameters.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper lists baseline code, packages, preprocessing, and hyperparameters, but I did not see a clear release link for PerturbODE itself or enough detail to reproduce all training choices, seeds, splits, and compute requirements.

Presentation is generally readable, but there are notable rough edges: placeholder-style citations such as 'Authors (2025)' and 'Available at [source if applicable]', typos, and some figures/tables that are difficult to interpret from the main text.

The impact/ethics statement is cursory for a genomics method. Potential misuse, clinical overinterpretation of inferred causal networks, dataset consent/privacy considerations, and risks of false biological discoveries are not meaningfully discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: scalable GRN discovery from large interventional single-cell datasets, especially TF overexpression settings where dynamics may matter.

The proposed model is biologically motivated, combining a neural ODE with decay terms, perturbation inputs, a low-rank/module factorization, and optimal-transport matching between initial and perturbed cell distributions.
The manuscript includes experiments on both simulated SERGIO data and a large real TF Atlas dataset, and it attempts comparisons against relevant differentiable causal discovery baselines.
The appendix provides useful implementation details, some ablations on number of perturbations and sparsity penalty, and a stability/generalizability analysis for selected TF Atlas edges.
weaknesses: The central causal GRN claims are not convincingly supported. The method is trained only to match endpoint distributions, and the paper acknowledges that distinguishing direct from indirect effects likely requires multiple time points. Yet it still presents the learned matrix as a causal GRN without adequate identifiability proof or validation.

Reported graph recovery performance is weak in absolute terms. On simulated yeast data, PerturbODE has AUPRC around 0.0044 and precision around 0.0046, while DCDI is better; on random DAGs, DCDI is again better. This makes the claimed GRN discovery capability much less convincing than the narrative suggests.

Thresholding and sparsity choices appear ad hoc and materially affect conclusions. The appendix says PerturbODE thresholds are chosen to predict a 'reasonable' number of edges, yet Table 3 shows massive overprediction, e.g. 43,655 edges for a 400-gene graph with 623 true edges and over 101,000 TF Atlas edges. This undermines interpretability and precision.

The TF Atlas evaluation is not sufficient for causal discovery. The benchmark contains only known positive edges, so the paper mainly reports recall and p-values against random graphs, without estimating false positives. A very dense graph can achieve high recall, and the manuscript’s own edge counts suggest this is a major concern.

The held-out intervention experiment is too limited and not fully convincing. It uses only 10 held-out TFs, compares primarily to weak linear SCM baselines because other methods cannot sample, and PerturbODE is worse than NO-TEARS-LR on several individual W2 cases despite a better mean. Stronger predictive baselines and more splits are needed.

The theoretical discussion is underdeveloped. The identifiability argument is deferred to an unpublished/placeholder 'Authors (2025)' reference and described as future work; this is not adequate support for the paper’s causal interpretation.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper cites baseline repositories but does not appear to provide PerturbODE code, trained models, or the modified SERGIO implementation. Several important choices, such as threshold constants and selected modules for biological interpretation, are hard to reproduce or audit.

Presentation has notable issues for a main-track submission, including placeholder/anonymized citations, typos, inconsistent claims about figures, and an overly perfunctory impact statement for a genomics method with possible biomedical implications.

strengths: Significant and timely problem: scalable GRN discovery from large perturbational single-cell datasets is important, and the paper targets a real gap between causal graph learners that scale poorly and trajectory models that do not use many interventions.

The proposed model is well motivated biologically: a low-rank/module neural ODE with sigmoid/Hill-like activation, decay terms, and intervention-specific inputs gives a plausible and interpretable parameterization, and the factorized GRN G = A diag(alpha) B is a useful design choice.

Empirical scope is reasonably strong: the paper evaluates on modified SERGIO simulations, random DAG simulations, and the large TF Atlas dataset, and includes comparisons to DCDFG, DCDI, NO-TEARS, NO-TEARS-LR, and Bicycle where feasible.

The unseen-intervention prediction results are compelling: PerturbODE obtains much higher Pearson correlation than the linear SCM baselines and lower average W2, with visual UMAP/PCA evidence supporting the quantitative results.

The appendices add useful detail on preprocessing, thresholds, hyperparameters, module counts, ablations, stability/generalizability, and gene enrichment. The stability analysis honestly reports that edge selection is only about 50-70%, which is helpful context rather than being hidden.
weaknesses: The causal-discovery evidence is not fully decisive. On SERGIO, PerturbODE does not outperform DCDI, and absolute AUPRC values are very low; on TF Atlas, evaluation is limited to positive curated edges, so precision and false discovery rates for real GRN inference remain largely unvalidated.

Several comparisons depend strongly on thresholding choices. PerturbODE thresholds are selected to yield a 'reasonable' number of edges, Bicycle thresholding is described as the only one yielding reasonable results, and Table 3 notes that PerturbODE tends to over-predict edges. This weakens confidence in the claimed GRN recovery superiority.

The strongest real-data GRN benchmark uses only three curated TF Atlas GRNs and recall/p-values against random graphs. This is useful but narrow, and random Erdos-Renyi baselines are not a very demanding null model for structured gene networks.

The unseen-intervention comparison is limited: DCDFG and DCDI are excluded for practical reasons, and the baselines are linear SCM sampling procedures that may not be competitive predictors of nonlinear cell-state distributions. Also, PerturbODE has very high variance in W2 and is worse than NO-TEARS-LR for several held-out TFs such as SETDB1 and TEAD1.

The identifiability discussion is incomplete. The paper acknowledges the issue but relies on an informal connection to related SDE results and future work; central causal claims would be stronger with clearer assumptions or theory for when the learned ODE parameters correspond to true regulatory edges.

Reproducibility is adequate but not complete. The manuscript gives many implementation details and cites baseline repositories, but I did not find a released PerturbODE code repository or a precise compute/runtime description. Some extracted appendix tables also appear inconsistent or duplicated, which should be checked.

The limitations and ethics discussion are thin. The paper notes future work on ATAC/ChIP-seq and multiple time points, but does not sufficiently discuss biological confounding, batch effects, off-target perturbation effects, uncertainty calibration, or downstream risks from incorrect regulatory-network claims.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: learning interpretable gene regulatory networks and perturbation dynamics from large-scale single-cell intervention data, especially TF Atlas-scale overexpression data where many existing causal discovery methods do not scale.

The proposed PerturbODE formulation is conceptually appealing: a neural ODE with a biologically motivated production/decay structure, explicit perturbation inputs, and a factorized module representation G = A diag(alpha) B that can be inspected as gene modules.

The manuscript evaluates on both modified synthetic simulators and a large real dataset, includes several relevant baselines for GRN inference and perturbation prediction, and reports useful appendices on hyperparameters, thresholding, module count, perturbation count, and stability/generalizability.

The real-data module analysis is biologically plausible: the inferred modules recover known developmental motifs from TF Atlas and show enrichment for anterior-posterior specification, trophoblast/vascular lineage programs, angiogenesis, and related pathways.
The broader impacts section is appropriately cautious that model-derived regulatory predictions require wet-lab validation before scientific or clinical use.
weaknesses: The central causal GRN discovery claims are not yet convincingly supported. On simulations, PerturbODE is not consistently best: DCDI substantially outperforms it on the 400-gene yeast SERGIO benchmark in recall/F1/AUPRC, DCDI and GENIE3 are competitive or better on 100-gene random DAGs, and NO-TEARS/GENIE3 outperform it on the small BoolODE case. The paper’s strongest claim is scalability, but the evidence for causal edge accuracy remains modest.

Absolute graph recovery quality is very low in several settings. For example, reported precisions and AUPRCs on SERGIO are often around 0.005-0.06, and ChIP-Atlas FDR remains roughly 50% even at medium/high thresholds. These numbers make the inferred GRNs difficult to rely on without stronger calibration, uncertainty estimates, or validation.

Real-data GRN evaluation is limited and potentially biased. The main TF Atlas reference GRNs contain only positive edges, so the paper reports recall and p-values rather than precision/AUPRC; threshold choices are manually adjusted to match sparsity or number of predicted edges; and the predicted TF Atlas graph is extremely dense in some settings, making recall advantages hard to interpret.

The held-out perturbation prediction result is mixed. PerturbODE beats linear SCM baselines and scGPT on W2, but GEARS has substantially better W2 distance on most held-out TFs and lower median W2 overall. PerturbODE also has very large errors on several TFs, so the claim that it accurately predicts unseen perturbations is overstated.

The identifiability discussion is weak for a causal discovery paper. The manuscript acknowledges that identifiability is delicate and appeals to an anonymous related result for a low-noise SDE variant, but does not prove or empirically diagnose when the learned ODE parameters or the factorized GRN are identifiable from endpoint distributions alone.

The biological/dynamical assumptions are not fully justified. The method learns trajectories from control to day-7 endpoint distributions without intermediate time points, so many dynamics can explain the same transport endpoint; this undercuts claims about recovering direct regulatory dynamics rather than fitting a distributional map.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives many hyperparameters and names public baseline implementations, but I did not see a clear release of PerturbODE code, preprocessing scripts, random seeds, exact train/test splits, or instructions sufficient to reproduce the TF Atlas experiments end to end.

Presentation is generally understandable but sometimes overclaims relative to the evidence, especially in phrases such as “causal,” “accurately predicts,” and “recovers appropriate gene network structure.” Some figures are hard to read in extracted form, and important quantitative values are embedded in plots rather than tables.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: scalable GRN discovery and perturbation-effect prediction from large single-cell perturbation datasets, where dynamics and intervention generalization are genuinely relevant.
The proposed model is conceptually interesting, combining a structured neural ODE, low-dimensional gene modules, explicit perturbation inputs, and an optimal-transport distributional loss.

The manuscript includes several useful empirical components: simulated GRN benchmarks, TF Atlas experiments, held-out intervention prediction, module enrichment analysis, ablations, stability checks, and compute/hyperparameter reporting.
The broader-impact discussion is appropriately cautious that predicted networks or intervention effects require wet-lab validation before scientific or clinical use.
weaknesses: The central causal/GRN discovery claims are not well supported. The model is trained mostly from endpoint distributions, not time-resolved trajectories, yet the paper makes strong claims about dynamics and direct causal regulatory edges. The discussion itself admits that identifiability is delicate and not rigorously shown for the proposed ODE setting.

Empirical GRN recovery is weak in absolute terms. On the 400-gene yeast SERGIO benchmark, PerturbODE reports AUPRC around 0.0045 and precision around 0.0079, while DCDI is substantially better. On random 100-gene DAGs, PerturbODE is comparable to GENIE3 but far below DCDI in AUPRC. These results do not justify the strong claims of robust GRN recovery.

The real-data GRN evaluation is fragile. The TF Atlas ground truths contain only positive edges, so the main metric is recall; this rewards dense graphs and cannot assess false positives. Table 3 shows PerturbODE predicts about 101k edges on 812 genes, and Table 1 still reports FDR around 50%. The reported p-values use Erdos-Renyi random graphs as a null, which is a weak baseline for biological networks and does not establish causal validity.

Thresholding and model-selection choices appear highly consequential and underjustified. Appendix A.6 states that thresholds are chosen differently across methods, sometimes to match ground-truth edge counts in simulations or to make GENIE3 and PerturbODE predict similar numbers of edges on TF Atlas. This makes the comparative graph metrics difficult to interpret.

The held-out intervention results are mixed and do not support the claim that PerturbODE accurately predicts unseen perturbations. GEARS has better W2 distance overall, PerturbODE has very large variance, and several individual TFs have severe failures. The evaluation uses only ten held-out TFs, with unclear split robustness.

The biological module analysis is suggestive but not decisive. Modules are selected post hoc by the highest overlap scores with known GRNs, pathway filters are restricted to relevant biological categories, and enrichment does not validate edge direction or direct regulation.

Presentation overstates the conclusions relative to the evidence. The abstract and conclusion claim efficacy, scalability, interpretability, and accurate unseen-intervention prediction, while the results show low absolute GRN precision/AUPRC, dense predictions, and unresolved identifiability.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper provides many hyperparameters and baseline repositories, but I did not find a release of the PerturbODE code, exact seeds, full split definitions, or enough implementation detail to reproduce the training pipeline and all thresholding/model-selection decisions reliably.

There are presentation and polish issues that reduce confidence, including placeholder-style citation text such as “Authors [2025]”, typos, repeated figure references, and some claims that are stronger than the corresponding experiments.

strengths: The paper proposes a useful and fairly original modeling framework for GRN discovery under perturbations: a neural ODE whose parameters factor through interpretable gene modules, trained with optimal transport between initial/control and perturbed cell-state distributions. This is a natural and biologically motivated way to combine dynamical modeling, perturbation information, and scalable network inference.

The method addresses an important practical gap. Existing differentiable causal discovery methods either impose DAG constraints that are biologically restrictive for GRNs or do not scale well to hundreds of genes and many perturbations; PerturbODE is explicitly designed for cycles, nonlinear interactions, and large TF perturbation datasets.

The empirical section is substantive. The authors evaluate on modified SERGIO and BoolODE simulations, a large TF Atlas setting with 812 genes, ChIP-Atlas validation, and held-out intervention prediction. The comparison set includes causal discovery baselines, GENIE3, GEARS, scGPT, and linear SCM/linear prediction baselines, which gives a reasonably broad picture.

The large-scale TF Atlas results are promising: PerturbODE* reports the best recall against the curated TF Atlas GRNs, the best AUPRC against ChIP-Atlas, and lower FDR than DCDFG at comparable sparsity. The module-level analyses and GSEA provide useful biological interpretability beyond aggregate scores.

The manuscript is generally clear and well structured. The equations, intervention variants, preprocessing, hyperparameters, and baseline implementations are described in meaningful detail, and the broader impact section appropriately cautions that predictions require wet-lab validation.
weaknesses: The central causal discovery claims are stronger than the evidence fully supports. Real-data validation relies on incomplete reference GRNs and ChIP-derived proxies, so high recall/AUPRC indicates biological plausibility rather than confirmed causal edge recovery. The paper acknowledges positive-only references in places, but the conclusion still leans heavily on causal GRN discovery language.

Synthetic results are mixed. PerturbODE is not consistently best: on BoolODE it is worse than NO-TEARS and GENIE3, on 100-gene SERGIO it is behind DCDI and GENIE3, and on the 400-gene yeast SERGIO benchmark DCDI has much higher recall/F1 despite scalability issues. This supports scalability and competitiveness more than clear state-of-the-art accuracy.

Held-out perturbation prediction is promising but not decisive. PerturbODE beats linear methods and scGPT on reported medians, but GEARS has substantially better W2 distance, and PerturbODE has very large failures for several held-out TFs such as SETDB1, POU2AF1, and TEAD1. The paper could use a deeper analysis of when these failures occur.

Evaluation depends substantially on thresholding and sparsity choices. The appendix explains threshold selection, but some choices are tuned to match ground-truth edge counts or comparable edge counts across methods, while TF Atlas predictions can be extremely dense. The reported FDRs around 50% on ChIP-Atlas also temper the practical reliability of inferred edges.

The identifiability discussion is underdeveloped. The paper states that identifiability should follow in the noiseless case from related SDE work when interventions exceed gene dimension, but no rigorous result is provided for this model. Given that the inferred GRN is extracted from a non-identifiable-looking factorization A diag(alpha) B, this is a material theoretical limitation.

Reproducibility is adequate but not complete. Many hyperparameters and public baseline repositories are listed, but I do not see a clear release of the PerturbODE code, exact random seeds/splits, or all details needed to reproduce the modified SERGIO/BoolODE perturbation simulations and TF Atlas preprocessing end to end.
